title: An eye for an eye
about: The one passage Ramchal uses to teach chapter 10's ascribed difficulty, and he names both of its key sentences himself (Heb p215, Eng p216). Of `תו קא קשיא לתנא` he says it is a `קשיא מגדת`, in which the reporter reports that the tanna felt this difficulty against his own words; of `אמרי, דנין` he says it is a difficulty against the report, showing the tanna cannot have meant it. Those two labels are therefore `attested`, and they are the only attested chapter 10 labels in the corpus.

What the passage is for: the composite is the one construct whose whole point is that a sentence does two jobs at once, and that cannot be seen from a definition. Here the difficulty is reported rather than raised, the report is attacked rather than the difficulty, the attack is turned with `אדרבה`, and the reserve derivation the baraita held back behind `אם נפשך לומר` turns out to have been held back for exactly this. The mishnah's ruling is never in question after the third sentence.

Text: Vilna, as Sefaria's William Davidson edition prints it. Ramchal's 1742 print reads `תו קא קשיא ליה לתנא`, with `ליה`; the Vilna text has none. The unit carries the Vilna reading and records his in a note rather than resolving the two.

units.speaker: Mishnah
units.short: damage is assessed in money, as for a slave
units.he: סימא את עינו, קטע את ידו, שיבר את רגלו – רואין אותו כאילו הוא עבד נמכר בשוק, ושמין כמה היה יפה וכמה הוא יפה
units.en: One who blinds another's eye is assessed as though the injured man were a slave sold in the market: we estimate what he was worth before and what he is worth now.

anatomy.note: `כאילו הוא עבד נמכר בשוק`: just as a slave's worth is assessed, so the injured man's. The known side is the slave market.
The mishnah fixes the injury by measure — what he was worth before and what he is worth now. The whole sugya turns on whether the Torah's `עין תחת עין` admits of measure at all.

units.short: say the verse means an actual eye
units.he: אמאי? ״עין תחת עין״ אמר רחמנא – אימא עין ממש!
units.en: Why money? The Merciful One said 'an eye for an eye' — say it means an actual eye.
units.note: A `דחיה`, not a `סתירה`: it does not show the mishnah false, only that the verse does not compel its reading. The literal possibility is left standing, which is what the rest of the passage has to close.

units.speaker: Baraita
units.short: just as striking an animal is paid for, so striking a man
units.he: לא סלקא דעתך; דתניא: יכול סימא את עינו – מסמא את עינו? תלמוד לומר: ״מכה אדם״ ו״מכה בהמה״; מה מכה בהמה – לתשלומין, אף מכה אדם – לתשלומין
units.en: That should not enter your mind. A baraita teaches: one might have thought that if he blinded an eye the court blinds his; the verse says 'one who strikes a person' and 'one who strikes an animal' — just as one who strikes an animal pays, so one who strikes a person pays.

anatomy.note: `מה … אף`: the rule is carried from the animal case to the human one on the shared word `מכה`.
The likeness is between two strikings, and it is the likeness the whole derivation rests on — which is why every later attack goes at it.

units.speaker: Baraita
units.short: the reserve derivation, from the ransom verse
units.he: ואם נפשך לומר, הרי הוא אומר: ״לא תקחו כפר לנפש רצח, אשר הוא רשע למות״ – לנפש רוצח אי אתה לוקח כפר, אבל אתה לוקח כפר לראשי אברים שאין חוזרין
units.en: And if you wish to say [that this can be objected to]: the verse says 'you shall not take ransom for the life of a murderer' — for a murderer's life you take no ransom, but you do take ransom for severed limbs, which do not grow back.

anatomy.note: The verse restricts the ban on ransom to a murderer's life; that the restriction is meant to exclude the limbs is read as forced, not merely suggested.
A life and a severed limb are held apart: the aspect the derivation turns on is that limbs do not grow back.

units.note: A second source brought beside the first for the same conclusion: `סיעתא`, not a fresh `הוכחה`. The baraita offers it without saying what is wrong with the first, and the Gemara will spend the last four sentences of the passage finding out.

units.short: which verse? not that one, it is about killing
units.he: הי ״מכה״? אילימא ״מכה בהמה ישלמנה, ומכה אדם יומת״ – ההוא בקטלא כתיב!
units.en: Which 'strikes'? If the verse 'one who strikes an animal shall pay, and one who strikes a person shall be put to death' — that one is written about killing.

anatomy.note: The obvious verse speaks of killing, not of injury — a different respect, so the two `מכה`s are not the same `מכה`.

units.note: The question and the elimination of the first candidate are one sentence in the text, so they are one unit. The move is an objection because it faults the derivation as given, not the ruling it supports.

units.he: אלא מהכא: ״מכה נפש בהמה ישלמנה״, וסמיך ליה: ״ואיש כי יתן מום בעמיתו״ … ״הכאה״–״הכאה״ קאמרינן; מה הכאה האמורה בבהמה – לתשלומין, אף הכאה האמורה באדם – לתשלומין
units.en: Rather from here: 'one who strikes an animal mortally shall pay', and juxtaposed to it 'if a man maims his neighbour, as he has done so shall be done to him'. The analogy is from striking to striking, not from the word: just as the striking said of an animal is for payment, so the striking said of a person.

anatomy.note: `מה … אף` again, but now from the act and not the word: the second verse never says `מכה`, and the derivation is allowed to rest on the juxtaposition instead.

`״הכאה״–״הכאה״ קאמרינן`: the injury verse says `יתן מום`, not `מכה`, and the settlement rests on the two being one matter — a striking — under different words. Ramchal's מאמרים נרדפים, `שמלותיהם שונות וענינם אחד` (Heb p211): a relation the wording concealed, here the analogy the objection said the word could not carry. It is the converse of what `hei-makkeh` found, one word `מכה` covering two matters, killing and injuring.

units.short: but that verse says he is put to death
units.he: והא כתיב: ״ואיש כי יכה כל נפש אדם, מות יומת״!
units.en: But it is written: 'and a man who strikes any person mortally shall be put to death'!
From where do you say it means money? Say it means actual death.

units.he: לא סלקא דעתך. חדא – דהא איתקש ל״מכה בהמה ישלמנה״. ועוד, כתיב בתריה: ״כאשר יתן מום באדם, כן ינתן בו״ – ושמע מינה ממון
units.en: That should not enter your mind. First, it is juxtaposed to 'one who strikes an animal shall pay'. And further, after it is written 'as he has given a blemish to a person, so shall it be given to him' — and 'given' means money.

anatomy.note: `חדא … ועוד`: two independent answers in one sentence, so a difficulty against either leaves the other standing. Ramchal's first branch of the conjoined compound, `בהשואה אחת` (Heb p33): the two grounds — the juxtaposition, and the word `ינתן` — are said on one footing, each a sufficient proof, neither the expected case and neither the news. The known-and-novel branch needs one part said `כמו ענין שכבר נודע` and the other `בדרך חדוש`, as alive against slaughtered in his firstborn example; `ועוד` adds a second reason of the same standing and does not rank it. That the juxtaposition was already used at `ela-mehacha` makes it familiar in the passage, not known in his sense, which is about how the parts stand to each other inside the sentence.
The first of the two is the same juxtaposition the settlement above already used.

commitment.note: the first reason: the juxtaposition to the striker of an animal, who pays
the second: `ינתן` means money — a ground of its own, so either can fall while the other stands

units.short: what was wrong with the first derivation?
units.en: And what is 'if you wish to say'? What difficulty with the first derivation did the baraita have in mind?
units.note: The baraita held a second derivation in reserve and never said why. The question is not whether the ruling is right — it is what the tanna was worried about.

units.short: the tanna's own unstated difficulty, reported
units.he: תו קא קשיא לתנא – מאי חזית דילפת ממכה בהמה? לילף ממכה אדם!
units.en: A further difficulty was troubling the tanna: what made you derive from 'one who strikes an animal'? Derive instead from 'one who strikes a person'!

anatomy.note: The move is a report and the payload is a difficulty. The Gemara does not raise this difficulty; it says the tanna felt it. Whether the ascription is right and whether the difficulty bites are two separate questions, and the next two sentences take them in that order.

units.note: Ramchal quotes this sentence and names it (Heb p215, Eng p216): `הנה זו קשיה מגדת שהגיד המגיד שהתנא הרגיש קשיה זו על דברי עצמו` — an ascribed difficulty, in which the reporter reports that the tanna felt this difficulty against his own words. He prints `תו קא קשיא ליה לתנא`; the Vilna text, carried here, has no `ליה`.

units.short: damages come from damages, not from death
units.he: אמרי: דנין ניזקין מניזקין, ואין דנין ניזקין ממיתה
units.en: They say: damages are derived from damages, and damages are not derived from death.

anatomy.note: Damages and death are held apart as domains: the objection is that a derivation must stay inside one.

units.note: Ramchal quotes this too and says what it does (Heb p215, Eng p216): `הנה הוא קשיה על הגדת המגיד – מראה שאי אפשר שתהיה זאת כונת התנא` — a difficulty against the report, showing the tanna cannot have meant this, since the answer was there for him to give. It lands on the ascription and leaves the mishnah's ruling entirely alone.

units.short: on the contrary: man from man, not from animal
units.he: אדרבה! דנין אדם מאדם, ואין דנין אדם מבהמה!
units.en: On the contrary — a person is derived from a person, and a person is not derived from an animal!

anatomy.note: `אדרבה` is Ramchal's own stock word for this move (Heb p137, Eng p138–140). The very principle that was supposed to settle the matter is turned round and sent back: if likeness of domain decides, likeness of subject decides the other way.
The same aspect as the objection it answers, read along the other axis — person against animal rather than damages against death. That both readings are available is the difficulty.

units.short: which is why the reserve derivation was there
units.he: היינו דקתני ״אם נפשך לומר״ – הרי הוא אומר: ״לא תקחו כפר לנפש רצח אשר הוא רשע למות״ – לנפש רוצח אי אתה לוקח כפר, אבל אתה לוקח כפר לראשי אברים שאינן חוזרין
units.en: This is just why the baraita taught 'if you wish to say': the verse says 'you shall not take ransom for the life of a murderer' — no ransom for a life, but ransom for severed limbs, which do not grow back.
units.note: The payoff. The tanna's unstated worry was real and has no answer, so his second derivation was not decoration: it is what the ruling rests on once the first is deadlocked. Nothing here touches the mishnah, which was never in doubt after the third sentence.
